pll1d15c7-d1e3477.summary: Answers that, besides the ineffable eternal generation, which some think could be called sending but is better called begetting, the Son is said to be sent in two ways: when he appeared visibly in flesh and when he passes into holy souls so as to be perceived and known.
claims: The eternal generation is properly called begetting, not sending.
The Son is sent visibly in flesh and invisibly into holy souls.

pll1d15c7-d1e3489.summary: Cites De Trinitate IV: the Son is said to be sent not by being born of the Father but by appearing as the Word made flesh, or by being perceived in time by a mind, as in 'send her (Wisdom) from heaven.' He is sent to each when known and perceived according to the capacity of a soul progressing toward God or perfect in God.
claims: The Son is not said to be sent by his eternal birth.
He is sent by appearing in flesh or by being perceived in a mind.
Invisible mission depends on the soul's capacity.

pl-l1d15c7.summary: Answers that, besides the eternal generation (which some call a sending, though it is better called begetting), the Son is sent in two ways: visibly, when he appeared in the flesh, and invisibly, when he enters holy souls so as to be perceived and known. Augustine distinguishes these: the Son is not said to be sent by being born of the Father, but by appearing as the Word made flesh, or by being perceived in time by someone's mind according to its capacity (Wis 9:10).
claims: The eternal generation is better called begetting than sending.
The Son is sent visibly in the incarnation.
The Son is sent invisibly when he is known and perceived by a holy soul.
Invisible mission is according to the capacity of the rational soul.
